prospect.name: Edward Garcia
prospect.occupation: Accountant with his own office; brutal tax season from end of January through April, working roughly 7am to 9-10pm for three months
prospect.family_status: Married; wife is about 15 years younger, is also an accountant, and recently had cosmetic surgery — which he names as a trigger: 'she's looking better, surgery-based. But I didn't want to kind of stay behind.' Two children aged 10 and 11. Multiple mortgages.
prospect.training_background: Played soccer through his late 30s including college soccer; boxing and kickboxing in his early 20s with a couple of returns since; CrossFit around 2018-2019 in his late 40s and 'in great shape' then, which died out with COVID. Nothing structured for at least two years. Currently does 30-40 minutes at home with dumbbells and a bench, plays soccer daily in the backyard with his kids, started dieting a few weeks ago and has gone 189 to 185 lb. Building a basement gym in the next couple of months.
prospect.medical: Chronic lower back trouble — 'my lower back has always been an issue' — improved by a year of regular stretching, now aches rather than pain, but flares if he forces it; he deliberately avoids deadlifts. No other conditions disclosed and none were asked about. Takes creatine, whey protein and 'detox vitamins'; reports bloating.

signals: Lost ground to a hard season and names it precisely: 'those few years right in COVID time, where I didn't do much... I let it go too much'
Wants a former self back — 'There are times in my life when I had agility and strength together, and I loved it... that was really more in my 30s than any other age'
Visible regret and a last-chance framing: 'I'm 56 years old, so this is kind of my last jump into it, I imagine. So I got to do it right'
Comparison wound driving the timing — his younger wife's recent surgery and 'I can't keep staying behind'
Counter-signal: he is not badly deconditioned and pushed back on being seen that way — 'I don't think I'm 240 pounds' — so he sits close to the optimizer line

goals.text: Lose 10-15 pounds of fat — 'my main goal is just lose 10-15 pounds and get fit'
Build actual muscle, especially chest and shoulders, without becoming bulky — 'I want to go straight to the muscle'
Regain agility and avoid stiffness — 'I'm not looking just to work out and get bulky... the main thing is the agility that you still keep, even though you could get to that muscle mass'
Fix the chronic lower back problem so it stops limiting what he can train
Build a habit that survives tax season so he stops cycling on and off — 'the goal is to somehow keep at it'
A home-based routine that takes little time, because gym trips take planning he will not sustain
Age well and stay functional — 'you have 70 year olds walking with a stick, but you also have 75 year olds still running around'
Keep up with a wife 15 years younger who has just had work done
Eventually return to recreational boxing once strength and agility are back
Finally reach a level of conditioning he has never reached — 'I never made it to that one stage of my life... I still have baby skin'

pains.text: Two years with no structured training and six years of mostly off rather than on
Tax season from end of January to April wipes out all discretionary time — 'February, March, and April, I just can't do anything else. Anything.'
Chronic lower back issue that dictates which exercises he will attempt
Desk-bound accountant with long hours and resulting stiffness
Needs external structure or he drifts — 'It's when I don't have anything organized that it's on and off, on and off'
No training peer group; friends his age are 'run down' and inconsistent, so there is no social pull
Daily liquid sugar — four or five spoons in drinks and soda at weekends and family events
Bores easily and needs things structured for him — 'I get bored super easily, right? So I have to have things set up for me to do'
Age anxiety about running out of runway — 'this is kind of my last jump into it'
Fear of falling behind his younger wife after her surgery
Tight household cashflow against multiple mortgages and two kids — 'we're full of bills'

objections.raw_quote: this is not pocket change, but how do I see something that I could be more assured that this is the program type of a thing? Because what I've seen is very little... Last night, I saw a little reel. Today, I got a phone call. I'm talking to you almost immediately.
objections.rep_response: Isolated it well — 'outside of that, you do feel like, yeah, this is something I see myself doing, it's just that you haven't seen that much of him yet. Is that correct?' — then admitted there is little more to show ('to answer the program aspects, there is not much more'), shared his screen to scroll Trevor's Instagram and client DMs, cited 1,000+ clients, and promised to send the link.

objections.raw_quote: I think I need to sleep over on this one, because I do have to discuss it with my wife anyway. It's not, it's not pocket change, right?
objections.rep_response: Joked about sleeping on the couch, agreed it is what married people do, then ran the personal-commitment isolation: 'do you personally feel like, yeah, I do want to make it work, and I see myself making it work?' Booked a specific follow-up call for the next day at 5pm and sent the invite live. Did not run the rest of the OB play.

objections.raw_quote: the numbers is a little high for what I was expecting to tell the truth. I'm not, I don't have any doubts on Trevor and in his program. I don't think that's the issue for me. The issue for me is the money part, because we're full of bills. So we had to make sure that I could make this bill.
objections.rep_response: Asked the right isolating question — 'is it more of like, I just don't want to do it all up front, or is it more so I just can't?' — and offered to split the payment, but ran no financial picture at all and let a confusing set of instalment numbers muddy the price.

objections.raw_quote: I could probably commit to the $3,000 for the first three months on $1,000 per month. I think I could do that once I speak to my wife. But I don't think I could do more than that.
objections.rep_response: Countered that instalments add $200 per payment, making it $3,600 over three months and $7,200 over six — above the ceiling the prospect had just named — and recommended the six-month option anyway.

objections.raw_quote: But yeah. I really got to think about it now.
objections.rep_response: Accepted it, reframed the follow-up as still worth having even if the money does not work ('even if it isn't doable at the moment, I would say let's just still jump on, because then we can maybe figure something out'), and locked a time.

offer.payment_plan_terms: Confused and internally contradictory as delivered. The rep first said splitting into three payments would carry no interest — 'if you feel like I do want to split it up, that we do it in three times. Then there wouldn't be any interest at it' — then immediately quoted instalments at $1,200/month, stating $3,600 for three months and $7,200 for six because 'when we do it in six times, it would add $200 per payment'. That is a $1,200 surcharge on the $6,000 six-month price. He verbally said '$36,000' and '$72,000' for those figures. The prospect noticed and challenged it: 'I don't understand, you said $6,000 before.'

evidence: Explicit deferral for spouse consultation: 'I think I need to sleep over on this one, because I do have to discuss it with my wife anyway'
No payment taken, no agreement sent, no meeting with Trevor booked
Strong process signal: a specific follow-up was booked for the next day at 5pm his time and the calendar invite was confirmed received live on the call
Positive signal on the programme itself: 'I don't have any doubts on Trevor and in his program. I don't think that's the issue for me. The issue for me is the money part.'
Positive signal on fit: 'The workout, me wanting to do the workout is not a problem'
Counter-evidence: he named a hard ceiling of $1,000/month and the instalment structure quoted lands at $1,200/month, above it

Counter-evidence: he flies out the next morning for a three-week holiday in Florida and the Dominican Republic, and the decision requires a joint sign-off with an accountant wife who has already suggested a cheaper route
outcome.next_step: Follow-up Zoom the next day at 5pm ET after he lands and settles at the resort, having discussed it with his wife that night; rep to send the Instagram link and text him from his personal number in the meantime.

notable.note: Two things to escalate. First, pricing: a three-month tier at $4,000 was quoted, which is not part of the $6,000/$9,000 structure, and the instalment terms were delivered so inconsistently that the prospect had to challenge them — no-interest-over-three-payments in one breath, a $200-per-payment surcharge in the next, with '$36,000' and '$72,000' said aloud for $3,600 and $7,200. The resulting $1,200/month sits above the $1,000/month ceiling the prospect had just stated, so the plan as quoted cannot close him. Second, the prospect asked a fair question the company could not answer — he wanted to see what the programme actually is before spending thousands, and the honest reply was 'there is not much more', followed by scrolling Instagram DMs on a screenshare. That is a collateral gap, not a rep failure. Also worth noting: he has a chronic lower back issue and avoids deadlifts, and nobody confirmed that a kettlebell programme built on hip hinges can accommodate that.
